sources.claim: Pull is a compound operation that first fetches and then integrates an upstream branch by the configured merge or rebase policy.

canonicalExplanation.summary: `git pull` is **two commands in one**: `git fetch`, then an **integration** of the upstream branch into yours. How it integrates depends on policy: **merge** (may create a merge commit), **rebase** (replays your local commits on top of the new upstream, giving them new hashes), or **fast-forward only** (refuses if you've diverged). Because pull integrates, it **can create commits, rewrite your unpushed commits, and cause conflicts**. So pull with a **clean working tree**, know your project's policy, and set it explicitly (`git config pull.rebase true` or `pull.ff only`) instead of relying on defaults.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner runs `git pull` on a branch with two local commits. Suddenly an editor opens asking for a merge message, and the history gains an unexpected merge commit that the project's rules forbid. A learner with a clean branch fetches, inspects divergence, and pulls with an explicit rebase policy required by the project. In this lesson you'll predict and perform a pull under an explicit policy in a disposable repository.

```predict
{"question": "Can git pull ever cause a conflict?", "options": ["No, it only downloads", "Yes: its second step merges or rebases, which can conflict"], "answer": 1, "why": "Pull = fetch + integrate. Integration is where conflicts happen."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Branches, merges and conflicts**, **Fetch and compare** and **Fast-forward and three-way merge**.

sections.heading: The rule: pull is fetch plus a chosen integration
sections.body:
```bash
git status                       # clean working tree first.
git fetch origin
git log --oneline --graph main origin/main -6   # see the divergence.

git pull --rebase origin main    # replay my commits on top of origin/main.
# or: git pull --ff-only         # refuse unless a fast-forward is possible.
# or: git pull --no-rebase       # merge, possibly with a merge commit.

git config pull.rebase true      # make the project's policy the default here.
```

| Policy | Diverged result | Rewrites local commits? |
|---|---|---|
| merge. | new merge commit. | no. |
| rebase. | linear; my commits replayed on top. | yes (new hashes). |
| ff-only. | refuses; you decide next. | no. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why is rebasing unpushed commits OK, but rebasing pushed ones risky?", "answer": "Rebase gives commits new hashes. If others already have the old ones, histories split. Local-only commits have no other copies, so replaying them is safe."}
```

examples.title: Pulling with the project's rebase policy
examples.situation: A learner with a clean branch fetches, inspects divergence, and pulls with an explicit rebase policy required by the project.
walkthrough: **Clean branch fetches:** git status is clean; git fetch shows main diverged 2 and 3.
**Inspects divergence:** the graph shows two local commits and three from the team.
**Pulls with an explicit rebase policy:** git pull --rebase replays the two commits on top; git log will show a straight line with no merge commit.
examples.result: History stays linear as the project requires, and no surprise commit appears.

examples.title: The ff-only safety net
examples.situation: A team sets pull.ff only. A learner's pull fails with "Not possible to fast-forward".
walkthrough: That means main has diverged from origin/main.
The learner fetches and inspects both log ranges.
They choose deliberately: rebase their unpushed work, or merge, per the team rule.
examples.result: No integration happens by accident; each one is a conscious choice.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Pull only downloads remote data and therefore cannot create commits, replay work, or cause conflicts.
misconceptions.correction: Pull fetches and then integrates. The merge step can create commits and conflicts, and the rebase step rewrites local commits.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, where did the unexpected merge commit come from?

analogy.example: Pulling is **collecting your mail and immediately filing it into your folders** in one go. Merge files the new letters next to yours with a cover note; rebase re-files your letters after the new ones; ff-only refuses if your folder has letters the post office doesn't know about.
limitations: Real filing rarely conflicts; overlapping code edits do.

remediation.explanation: Before pulling, answer three questions: **Is my tree clean? What does fetch show? Which policy applies here?**

recap.summary: To pull predictably, remember pull is fetch followed by merge, rebase or fast-forward-only integration, so start from a clean tree, fetch and inspect divergence first, and use the project's explicit policy, knowing integration can create commits, replay local work or cause conflicts.
